newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: FEATURE-Crackdown demoralises Bahrain's restless Shi'ites.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Crackdown demoralises Bahrain's restless Shi'ites.

text.p: Women in black shawls and teenagers knelt on the dirt and sprinkled rose water on the grave of Isa Qamber, a Bahraini Shi'ite convicted of killing a policeman.
They raised their fists and shouted slogans in support of their imprisoned and exiled leaders.
Minutes later a few helmeted security men in green uniforms arrived clutching rifles at Bahrain's al-Houra cemetery. The crowd fell silent.
Three youths were lined up against a wall and struck with a truncheon by one of the security men. Then the crowd was ordered to leave.
Such incidents continue to fuel Shi'ite anger in Bahrain, the Gulf's financial and banking centre, where at least 27 people have died in political unrest since December 1994.

Members of Bahrain's majority Shi'ites have waged a violent campaign to demand political and economic reforms -- including job opportunities and the restoration of an elected parliament dissolved by the government in 1975.
The Sunni-led government says the protesters are out to destabilise Bahrain and blames Iran for much of the unrest.
"The violence has no relation whatsoever to the parliament," insists a government official. "These are people who want to destabilise Bahrain. They are terrorists.
"Iran is backing much of the violence," the official told Reuters.
A widespread security crackdown by the government has disheartened the Shi'ite opposition, according to members of the Shi'ite community and Western diplomats.
They also say morale in the restless Shi'ite community has sunk to its lowest level since the trouble flared.
"There is nothing we can do right now. We are weaker than ever before. We are a people without leaders," said one Shi'ite opposition figure who requested anonymity.
Influential leaders such as Sheikh Abdul-Amir al-Jamri remain imprisoned along with scores of activists.

Diplomats estimate the government has rounded up 1,000 political prisoners. Opposition circles give a far higher figure of around 2,500 in jail but a government official told Reuters they numbered just a few hundred.

Qamber was shot by firing squad earlier this year in the first execution connected with the political violence. Three other Shi'ite activists have been condemned to death for firebombing a restaurant, killing seven Bangladeshi workers.

Exiled leaders are struggling to stir up the kind of anti-government fury that in the past unleashed arson attacks, bombings, protests and sabotage and prompted the army to hint it would impose martial law to crush the dissent.
Diplomats say the turning point came in June when Bahrain accused Iran of plotting an armed revolt and arrested 56 Bahrainis. Tehran denied the charge.
"The announcement was a way to say to the Shi'ites now it's over," said one Western diplomat. "It was a message to those who were planning further unrest."

Security forces with automatic weapons patrol Manama and highways ringing Shi'ite villages in black-painted vehicles. Other security forces cruise the streets and alleys of villages in blue trucks mounted with searchlights.
"We are scared to go out. Now if a small group of people gather, the security people will come immediately," said one villager, shortly before a patrol drove by.
Diplomats predict the government will continue to contain the violence for at least the next year as it moves to improve the economic climate and job prospects.
The government says it will create 8,000 new jobs next year to help ease the unemployment problem.
Most of the jobless among Bahrain's 580,000 population are members of the Shi'ite community who live in villages that have been hotbeds of the unrest.
"The Shi'ites will continue to pose a problem in the long term without political and economic reform," concluded one diplomat.
